introduction-how-do-we-know-its-working.core: Without measurement, platform teams can't prove value or know what to improve. Combine DORA (delivery performance), SPACE (developer experience and productivity) and adoption metrics (product health) for a full picture.

first_principles.problem: Leadership asks whether the platform team's investment paid off, and the team has only anecdotes.

analogy.title: A car's dashboard
analogy.story: Speed (delivery), engine health (developer wellbeing) and fuel usage (adoption) together tell you how the journey's going.
analogy.breaks: Metrics can be gamed, so use them for learning, not punishment.

example.title: A platform review with metrics
flow: After: lead time −55%, dev satisfaction +20, adoption 72%

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Funding and priorities based on evidence.

check.q: Why do platform teams need metrics?
check.a: To demonstrate value, guide prioritisation and detect whether changes actually help developers.

dora-metrics-the-industry-standard-for-d.core: DORA's four key metrics are deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service (with reliability added later). They measure throughput and stability together, and research links them to organisational performance.

first_principles.problem: Teams measure activity (commits, tickets) instead of delivery outcomes.
truths: Speed and stability aren't trade-offs for elite performers.
Outcome metrics resist gaming better than activity metrics.
derivation: **Change failure rate**: % of deploys causing issues.

analogy.title: A delivery company's performance
analogy.story: How often trucks leave, how long delivery takes, how many packages arrive damaged and how fast you fix mistakes.
analogy.breaks: DORA measures delivery, not whether you're building the right thing.

example.title: Computing DORA from tooling
flow: Lead time: commit timestamp → deploy timestamp

check.q: What are the four DORA metrics?
check.a: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service.

the-space-framework-measuring-the-human-.core: SPACE (Satisfaction and well-being, Performance, Activity, Communication and collaboration, Efficiency and flow) captures developer productivity across several dimensions, because great DORA numbers can coexist with burnout and frustration.

first_principles.problem: A team deploys 30 times a day with good DORA scores, but engineers are exhausted and planning to quit.
truths: Self-reported and system data complement each other.
derivation: **Satisfaction**: surveys on tools, processes and burnout.
**Communication** and **efficiency/flow**: interruptions, handoffs, focus time; pick metrics from **at least 3 dimensions**.

analogy.title: A health check-up
analogy.story: Not just weight, but blood pressure, sleep, mood and fitness together.
analogy.breaks: Activity metrics alone (lines of code) are harmful, which SPACE explicitly warns against.

example.title: A SPACE dashboard
flow: Insight: speed at the cost of burnout

check.q: Why is SPACE needed in addition to DORA?
check.a: DORA measures delivery; SPACE captures human factors like satisfaction, flow and collaboration that sustain performance.

adoption-metrics-treating-the-platform-a.core: Adoption metrics show whether the platform is used and valued: percentage of services or teams on golden paths, active users of portal features, time-to-first-deploy for new services, retention (teams staying on the platform) and NPS.

first_principles.problem: The platform launched features nobody uses, and the team doesn't know it.
truths: Funnels show where users drop off.
derivation: **Engagement**: weekly active users of the portal or CLI.

analogy.title: A SaaS product dashboard
analogy.story: Signups, activation, daily active users and churn, applied to an internal product.
analogy.breaks: Mandated adoption inflates numbers, so measure satisfaction too.

example.title: An adoption funnel

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The biggest friction point is targeted.

example.outcome: the platform managed with product data.

check.q: What does 'time to first deploy' measure for a platform?
check.a: How quickly a new service or team gets value, which is the activation stage of adoption.

connecting-the-three-frameworks-a-unifie.core: Adoption is the leading indicator (are teams using it?), SPACE shows the experience (is it helping people?) and DORA the outcomes (is delivery improving?). Together they tell a causal story from platform investment to business results.

first_principles.problem: Teams report metrics in isolation and can't explain how platform work leads to better outcomes.
truths: Metrics can conflict, which is informative.

analogy.title: Fitness, health and race results
analogy.story: Training consistency (adoption) improves fitness (experience), which improves race times (outcomes).
analogy.breaks: Correlation isn't proof, so look for corroborating evidence and qualitative feedback.

example.title: A quarterly platform report
flow: Narrative: paved road → less friction → faster delivery

check.q: How do adoption, SPACE and DORA metrics relate?
check.a: Adoption is a leading indicator, SPACE reflects the improved experience, and DORA shows the resulting delivery outcomes.
